prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, and the colleagues' ballots have strengthened rather than weakened that view. It is the only candidate here that six of seven rankers placed in their top three, so the support is broad and not driven by one subfield. The discovery is nature-led in the sense I care about: a sharp quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) that a specific twist angle should flatten the bands, followed seven years later by an experiment (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) that found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. That is the committee's usual pattern of theory anticipating a surprise and experiment confirming it. The field it opened has been reproduced across many groups and platforms, and the core observations are robust even though the pairing mechanism is still debated. The credited names also give a clean trio of one theory pair and one experimental leader, which is rarer than it looks among the other candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing and attribution. Eight years is short, the mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of several correlated phases remain open, and several colleagues (Eriksson, Johansson, Olsson, Pearce) flag this. Attribution is also imperfect: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, is outside the credited names, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, as well as later groups such as Dean, Young and Yazdani, shaped the field. If the committee regards the physical interpretation as too unsettled, a more mature candidate such as optical lattice clocks or IceCube would be the safer prize, and I cannot dismiss that argument.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as atomic physics at its purest: a clear measurement-limited advance at the 10^-18 level, confirmed by many groups, with a clean Katori and Ye pairing and a pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B036 is the cleanest attribution on the list and that the maturity is not in doubt, which is why I keep it as my first alternative and not far down. My disagreement is about what kind of achievement the prize should mark. The clocks are an extraordinary refinement of a technique whose conceptual root, the frequency comb and laser cooling, has already been honoured in 2005 and 2001, whereas twisted bilayer graphene is a new phenomenon that nobody expected from carbon. I also do not think the pending SI redefinition adds scientific weight to the discovery itself. If the committee prefers a precision-measurement prize, I would not oppose it, but I would not put it above a genuine opening of a new field.

responses.point: Eriksson puts the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect first because topology, not symmetry breaking, became an organising principle of band structure, with strong confirmation in many materials, while placing magic-angle graphene third as possibly premature.
responses.response: Eriksson's conceptual argument for B054 is serious and I ranked it fourth myself. My qualification is that the 2016 prize already recognised topological phases of matter, so a topological-insulator prize would partly revisit that ground, and the credited trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and the late Shoucheng Zhang, who made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's group tested. That is a real gap in a prize built on prediction plus experiment. On timing for B022 I accept the risk Eriksson names, but the experimental phenomena have been reproduced across many devices and materials, and the open question is the mechanism, not whether the effects exist. I think that is early but defensible, and I do not agree it is more premature than the attribution gap in B054.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson first as one of the clearest and most consequential measurements in modern physics, independently confirmed by two experiments, and argues it is arguably overdue since the 2013 prize covered only the theory.
responses.response: As a high-energy theorist I do not underrate the Higgs discovery; its importance is not the question. Two things hold me back. First, the credited set of four is a founders-and-spokespersons list from collaborations of thousands, and Pearce himself says the choice among four names is contestable, so any three-person cut will be hard to defend as the decisive contributors. Second, only Pearce and Lindroth ranked it, at first and seventh, so it has the thinnest support of any serious candidate. I would take it seriously if the committee can agree on a principled way to credit a collaboration, but nothing in the ballots so far provides one, and I would not make it my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the jamming transition first as a unifying statistical-mechanical account of rigidity in disordered athermal matter, conceptually clean with two decades of numerical and experimental confirmation and a natural Liu and Nagel pairing.
responses.response: I find the jamming case conceptually attractive and appreciate that Mehlig also ranks B022 second, so we are not far apart. My reservation is whether jamming is a single sharply defined discovery of nature or a unifying framework whose universality class and relation to glass physics Mehlig himself notes are still debated. Opening support is just one first place with no one else ranking it, which tells me the other members have not yet been persuaded it has the decisive experimental or theoretical landmark a prize needs. I would like to hear which specific result he would cite as the discovery in the citation text.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unsettled pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene as a maturity problem; I have not verified the current state of the field.
Whether the omission of Yuan Cao and the many other contributors to the 2018 experiments is acceptable under the three-person limit.
Whether a precision-measurement prize such as B036 or a new-window prize such as B012 would be preferred by colleagues if B022 is judged too early.
How the committee should credit a large collaboration if the Higgs experimental discovery or IceCube is pursued.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My research is in string theory, gravity and cosmology, and none of the shortlisted candidates involves my PhD supervisor David Gross, my mentor Hector Rubinstein, my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet or the Uppsala theory group. My two years at CERN were in the 1990s, well before the ATLAS and CMS discovery, and I do not regard that as a recusal issue for B017.
